title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Problem (J. A. Euler, fragment 100, begun on p. 497). Take the hyperbola n y = sqrt(2ax + x^2), i.e. (x+a)^2 - n^2 y^2 = a^2. Its semi-axis is a, its conjugate semi-axis is a/n, and the asymptote CN makes tan ACN = 1/n with the axis. The fragment seeks the limit of the excess of the asymptote segment CN over the arc AM as M goes to infinity.

First method (from the previous page). Substituting tan phi = t gives CN - AM = a n * Integral_{1/n}^{inf} t/sqrt(n^2 t^2 - 1) * (1 - t/sqrt(1+t^2)) dt. Expanding 1 - (1 + t^-2)^(-1/2) in powers of 1/t gives
CN - AM = n a * sum_k (-1)^k [(2k+1)!!/(2k+2)!!] I_{2k+1}, where I_{2k+1} = Integral dt/(t^{2k+1} sqrt(n^2 t^2 - 1)).

On this page, put t = 1/u. Then I_{2k+1} = Integral_0^n u^{2k} du / sqrt(n^2 - u^2). Euler sets up the reduction formula with an undetermined algebraic term:
Integral -u^{l+2}/sqrt = A * Integral -u^l/sqrt + B u^{l+1} sqrt(n^2 - u^2).
Here A = (l+1) n^2/(l+2) and B = 1/(l+2). The boundary term vanishes at u = 0 and u = n. This gives the Wallis values I_{2k+1} = [(2k-1)!!/(2k)!!] (pi/2) n^{2k}. Hence
CN - AM = (pi/2) n a [1/2 - (1^2/2^2)(3/4) n^2 + (1^2 3^2/2^2 4^2)(5/6) n^4 - ...].
In modern terms this is (pi/4) a n * 2F1(1/2, 3/2; 2; -n^2), which converges for n <= 1.

Second, 'more elegant' method. Put m = n^2/(1+n^2) and u^2 = a^2/(n^2 y^2 + a^2). Then y = (a/n) sqrt(1-u^2)/u and dy = -(a/n) du/(u^2 sqrt(1-u^2)), so
CN - AM = -(a/sqrt m) Integral_1^0 (1 - sqrt(1 - m u^2)) du / (u^2 sqrt(1-u^2)).
Integrating by parts with sqrt(1 - m u^2) d(sqrt(1-u^2)/u), the boundary terms vanish at u = 1 and at u -> 0 (there sqrt(1 - m u^2) is about 1 - m u^2/2). The result is
CN - AM = a sqrt(m) Integral_0^1 sqrt(1-u^2)/sqrt(1 - m u^2) du = a [E(k) - (1 - k^2) K(k)]/k, with k^2 = m = 1/e^2 (e the eccentricity).
This is an expression by conic-section rectification. Euler refers to Novi Comm. VIII p. 134, case II.

The next page expands this integral into (pi/4) a sqrt(m) 2F1(1/2, 1/2; 2; m). Together the two series are an instance of Pfaff's transformation with z = -n^2 and z/(z-1) = m. I checked the agreement to order n^3: both give (pi/4) a n (1 - 3n^2/8).
errors: No substantive errors. I verified the substitution t = 1/u, the reduction formula (B = 1/(l+2), which the text leaves implicit), the Wallis values, both forms of the series coefficients (e.g. 3/16 and 15/128), the substitution dy, the integration by parts and the vanishing of the boundary terms.
'valde convergit' for n < 1 is optimistic. The coefficients decay only like 1/(pi k), so convergence is fast only for small n and slow as n -> 1.

ideas.what: Reduction formula for Integral u^{l+2}/sqrt(n^2 - u^2) via an undetermined algebraic term, giving the Wallis integrals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Wallis; Euler's standard method (Institutiones calculi integralis)
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi integralis I (E342), reduction chapters

ideas.what: Limit of the difference between the asymptote and the hyperbolic arc expressed as a power series in n (ratio of the axes)
ideas.modern_name: Series for the asymptote-minus-arc constant of the hyperbola (2F1 series)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Landen (1771/1775) for the asymptote-arc difference via elliptic arcs; Maclaurin for hyperbola-ellipse arc relations
ideas.where_published: Possibly in Euler's elliptic-arc papers; the page itself cites Novi Comm. VIII p.134

ideas.what: Integration by parts reducing the asymptote-arc limit to a complete integral Integral_0^1 sqrt(1-u^2)/sqrt(1-mu^2) du, i.e. a rectification of a conic
ideas.modern_name: Complete elliptic integrals: (E - k'^2 K)/k with k = 1/e
ideas.where_published: The page cites Novi Comm. T. VIII p.134 cas. II (exact E-number unsure)

missed.claim: This series and the one on the next page are two hypergeometric expansions of the same quantity. Equating them is an instance of Pfaff's transformation, 2F1(1/2,3/2;2;-n^2) = (1+n^2)^(-1/2) 2F1(1/2,1/2;2;n^2/(1+n^2)). It is obtained here geometrically, but Euler and Pfaff knew such transformations, so this is of minor interest only.
missed.quote: Sequenti autem modo hoc problema elegantius solvetur.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical illustration only; it is not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries out a correct but standard computation: Wallis integrals, binomial series and reduction to a complete elliptic integral. It deals with a classical problem (asymptote minus hyperbolic arc) that Landen and Euler treated in print and that the text itself refers to Novi Comm. VIII. Nothing appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: In the integration-by-parts line, the radical in the image appears to extend over both factors: sqrt((1-uu)(1-muu))/u rather than sqrt(1-uu)*(1-muu)/u. Only the former is mathematically correct, both in the line 'habebimus' and in the line 'hincque'.
'ubi terminus algebraicus fit = 0 tam si u=n quam si u=0' — the transcription is correct. The coefficient B (= 1/(lambda+2)) is never stated explicitly.
